explain.say: Imagine reading a book where every sentence is tiny. I woke up. I ate. I ran. It sounds like a robot! Look at the board. The first box holds a short sentence: It was raining. Let's join it to another one.

explain.say: See the second box? That is a joining word, called a conjunction. It works like glue between ideas. The common ones are and, but, so and because. Which one would you pick for rain and umbrella?

explain.say: Each glue word means something different. Look at the board now. And adds, or gives a choice. But and yet show a surprise. So and because show a result or a reason. Can you finish this: I was tired, but...

faq.a: A conjunction is a joining word, like and, but, so or because. It links words, ideas or two sentences together.

faq.q: How do I join two sentences?
faq.a: Pick a joining word that shows how the ideas connect, then put it between them: It was cold, so I wore a coat.
asks: How do I make a longer sentence?

faq.q: Can you start a sentence with because?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the sentence has both parts: Because it rained, we stayed inside. Because it rained on its own is not a full sentence.
asks: Is it wrong to start with because?

faq.a: FANBOYS helps you remember seven joining words: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. They join two equal ideas.

faq.q: Do I need a comma before and or but?
faq.a: When and, but or so join two full sentences, writers often put a comma before it: I was hungry, so I ate a banana.

facts: The seven coordinating conjunctions are for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so: FANBOYS.
And is one of the five most common words in written English.

quiz.say: I wanted to play outside, blank it was too dark.
quiz.show: I wanted to play outside, ___ it was too dark.
quiz.why: But shows the second part goes against the first.

wrong.0: so would mean the dark was a result of wanting to play.
wrong.1: and adds an idea; it does not show the surprise.

quiz.why: Because tells you why: I smiled because I won.
